title: Limitys: overlapping sequences, continual forgetting, and protected routing
summary: September 26 turns the sequence-overlap intuition into a matched continual-learning comparison. Limitys trains five phases of mutually conflicting sequence endings with no replay and compares a plain GRU, a learned context gate, an anatomy-shaped microcircuit, and a fixed random context mask. All learned-routing arms learn the newest phase perfectly but collapse to the same 0.233 all-phase junction retention; the fixed mask retains 0.793. The preregistered anatomy-beats-generic-gate claim fails in 0/5 seeds. The useful survivor is narrower: gating alone is not memory protection. Stable context-to-subspace assignments can prevent later learning from overwriting earlier sequence distinctions, separating runtime admission from slower protected routing.

nodes.claim: Tests whether an anatomy-shaped apical/SST/PV/AIS-like control circuit preserves overlapping sequences learned sequentially better than a plain GRU or a generic learned context gate, under matched parameter counts and no replay.
nodes.survived: Every arm learned the newest phase at 1.00 accuracy, but only the fixed random context mask protected old endings: all-phase junction retention was 0.793 for the fixed mask versus 0.233 for the plain GRU, learned gate, and anatomical microcircuit. The result isolates stable context-to-subspace assignment as the useful ingredient in this task: later phases cannot freely take over units reserved for earlier contexts.
nodes.killed: The anatomical microcircuit did not beat the learned generic gate or the plain GRU; MICRO minus GATE was 0.000 in 0/5 seeds, and all three learned-routing systems overwrote old endings completely. The experiment therefore does not support apical gating, slow SST-like inhibition, PV-like normalization, or AIS-like release as sufficient mechanisms for continual sequence retention. A fixed anatomical mapping was not tested, and if it works the credit belongs to the protected mapping rather than the biological labels.

edges.why: KolmeOvea separates apical/context, basket/perisomatic timing, and chandelier/AIS publication surfaces. Limitys asks whether an anatomy-shaped version of that control decomposition actually protects sequentially learned overlapping memories; in this task it does not, shifting the useful requirement from fast control surfaces to stable protected routing.

Rytmi asks how ordered sequence trajectories can be written and replayed. Limitys moves to the next failure mode: many conflicting trajectories are learned one after another, and the question becomes whether old branch structure survives later learning.
